frameworks.name: Debt Recombination Model
frameworks.definition: A strategic framework for choosing which type of business debt (financial, operational, talent, infrastructure, tech) to incur at each stage based on what the founder can most easily repay.

frameworks.name: Cash Flow Acceleration Variables
frameworks.definition: A set of four independent levers for improving business cash flow: acquire customers cheaper, get them to pay faster, get them to pay more, and scale execution through hiring.

claims.text: Founders get disproportionately compensated relative to early employees because founders must perform multiple roles well and absorb the debt that the business incurs (Alex Hormozi). Founders take larger risks with their personal effort and resources, earning returns proportional to that risk-taking.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founders absorb operational, talent, infrastructure, and tech debt that would otherwise require cash compensation; when the business succeeds, they capture the upside proportional to risks taken.
bounded_by: Does not apply to funded startups that can pay market rates for specialized talent from day one

claims.text: Every business incurs debt; the strategic question is which type of debt to incur. Bootstrapped businesses actively choose not to incur financial debt but must incur operational debt, talent debt, infrastructure debt, and tech debt instead (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Funded businesses can trade financial debt for reduced operational debt

claims.text: For bootstrapped businesses with limited cash flow, the choice to hire a growth-focused salesperson requires betting the founder's full salary/compensation on that single hire succeeding, because cash flow severely constrains hiring capacity (Alex Hormozi). The alternative is to backfill your own current work first, then redirect freed time and cash toward acquiring a reliable sales channel.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Limited cash flow means a single expensive hire represents 100% of the cash available for hiring, creating binary success/failure outcomes. Backfilling removes the all-or-nothing bet by freeing the founder's time first.
bounded_by: Does not apply to funded businesses with capital reserves
Does not apply to businesses with healthy cash flow (>$1M+ annually)

claims.text: The best growth practitioners ("rainmakers") do not need founders and can succeed independently; they will only join a bootstrapped business if the vision and equity stake is sufficiently compelling to justify foregoing higher cash compensation (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Top performers have alternative opportunities; they will accept lower cash compensation only if the upside (equity, vision, growth trajectory) is substantially more valuable than cash elsewhere.
bounded_by: Does not apply to highly specialized or commodity roles where cash compensation is the primary draw

claims.text: Cash flow is the oxygen of the business. Improving cash flow unlocks the ability to hire, scale, and grow; conversely, constrained cash flow creates a ceiling on what the founder can do without external capital (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to heavily funded businesses with capital reserves

claims.text: For a training company with $2M revenue (20% margins = $400k free cash flow) and $10M ambitions, hiring one full-time "stud" employee exhausts annual cash flow, creating high risk if the hire underperforms (Alex Hormozi). This risk explains why founders are compensated more — they absorb larger bets.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: Revenue stage and cash flow capacity for hiring

anchors.value: $400k annual free cash flow = capacity for ~1 full-time hire at market rate
scales hiring capacity proportionally if margins maintained

bounded_by: Assumes 20% net margins; higher margins improve capacity

claims.text: If a bootstrapped founder increases revenue and cash flow from $2M to $2.5M (e.g., by working overtime), that additional $100-150k cash flow enables hiring a second person without exhausting all available capital, creating organizational lift-off (Alex Hormozi). The founder works harder short-term to afford the hire, the hire then multiplies output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder capacity to work additional hours
claims.mechanism: Additional cash flow ($100-150k) enables hiring without capital injection. The new hire multiplies the founder's output, creating a compounding growth cycle.

numbers.axis: Revenue threshold for sustainable second hire

anchors.value: ~$400k cash flow; exhausted by one market-rate hire
~$500-550k cash flow; can sustain two hires with founder working overtime

bounded_by: Assumes founder is willing to work overtime
Assumes hire is deployed toward revenue-generating activity

claims.text: SEO and word-of-mouth are unreliable as a business's only customer acquisition channels because SEO is being eroded by AI (ChatGPT, Claude) and word-of-mouth provides no predictable volume (Alex Hormozi). A bootstrapped business should prioritize establishing a reliable, paid acquisition channel (e.g., corporate sales outreach, ads) that the founder can control.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses reliant solely on SEO or word-of-mouth
bounded_by: SEO may remain viable for certain niches not yet impacted by AI
Word-of-mouth can be a supplement to, not primary, acquisition channel

claims.text: The founder should backfill their own current work (hire someone to replace what the founder is doing today) before hiring a growth person. Backfilling enables the founder to redirect all freed time and capital toward building a new, reliable sales channel, which creates more leverage than hiring a rainmaker without a channel (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to founder-facing roles (customer relationship, product vision) that cannot be delegated

claims.text: In a B2B training business, corporate training deals have significantly higher ticket price than individual open-enrollment trainings. If the founder can reliably sell 10 corporate engagements per week through a repeatable sales channel, there is no operational constraint preventing scaling to 10 per week — the function scales identically, just with proportionally higher revenue (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The operational function (closing a corporate training deal) remains identical at 1 deal/week or 10 deals/week. Scaling is additive on a system that already exists, not multiplicative complexity.
bounded_by: Assumes delivery infrastructure can scale to meet demand
Assumes sales process is truly repeatable and not founder-dependent

claims.text: Focusing on a single revenue stream (B2B corporate training) rather than splitting effort between B2B corporate and B2C individual enrollments likely produces faster growth due to operating leverage — the unit economics and sales motion scale more efficiently when focused (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: training company with mature B2B and B2C channels
B2B has higher ticket and margin
bounded_by: Does not apply if B2C revenue is proportionally higher
Does not apply if operational constraints are not channel-specific

examples.text: A training company founder is considering how to scale from $2M to $10M revenue with limited cash flow ($400k annually at 20% margins). The founder's instinct is to hire a top salesperson who can drive growth, but this would consume the entire year's free cash flow in a single hire. Instead, Hormozi recommends the founder first hire someone to replace the founder's own current work (operational backfill), then use the freed-up time to establish a reliable corporate sales channel. Once that channel exists, the founder can then hire additional salespeople to execute the channel at scale. This sequencing — backfill → channel → salespeople — avoids the high-risk single bet of hiring a growth person without first establishing a repeatable sales motion.

Hormozi notes that top performers in sales and growth ('rainmakers') typically have the skills to succeed independently and do not need a founder. They will only join a bootstrapped company if the founder's vision is compelling enough and the equity stake is sufficiently valuable that it justifies accepting lower cash compensation. This is why founders with limited cash must focus on selling the *vision* and *equity*, not cash, to attract A-players.

A $2M revenue training company with 20% margins generates roughly $400k in free cash flow annually. Hiring a single market-rate employee at ~$100-150k fully-loaded (salary + benefits) consumes 25-40% of this cash flow. Hiring a second employee would require the founder to increase total revenue by an additional $500k (to reach $2.5M, generating ~$100k more cash flow), which could be achieved by the founder working overtime on revenue-generating activities. This illustrates the tight cash flow constraint at the $2M stage.

practices.text: Establish a reliable, repeatable acquisition channel (such as structured corporate sales outreach, paid advertising, or partnership development) as your first priority before hiring additional salespeople. This channel becomes the throughput multiplier for all subsequent hiring.

When bootstrapped, hire for backfill (replacing your current work) before hiring for growth. Backfill employees should be lower-cost specialists in your current role; growth hires are expensive and risky without a proven channel.

Focus all business effort and resources on the revenue stream with the highest ticket price and margin (e.g., B2B corporate training over B2C individual enrollments) to maximize operating leverage and cash flow at early stages.
